baseline_protocol:
Age: 5  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Spreading rash around the mouth and nose with honey-colored crusted lesions for 5 days, without systemic symptoms.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation is consistent with impetigo, a superficial bacterial skin infection commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. Key diagnostic features include well-defined erosions with characteristic golden-yellow (honey-colored) crusts, perinasal and perioral distribution, and presence of satellite lesions. The history of similar sores in daycare contacts supports a contagious etiology. Absence of fever, systemic symptoms, deep tissue involvement, or fluctuance argues against cellulitis, abscess, or deeper infection. No history of eczema or immunodeficiency reduces likelihood of atypical or severe presentations. Differential diagnoses include herpes simplex virus (clustered vesicles, fever more common), candidiasis (less crusting, more common in moist areas), and allergic dermatitis (pruritus, no honey-colored crusts), but these are less consistent with the described findings.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: The child has localized, nonbullous impetigo, likely transmitted in a daycare setting, with typical clinical features and no signs of systemic illness or complications.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  
Recommendations: Treat with topical antibiotic therapy (e.g., mupirocin ointment applied to lesions three times daily for 7–10 days). For lesions that are extensive or not responding to topical therapy, consider oral antibiotics active against Staphylococcus and Streptococcus (e.g., cephalexin or clindamycin). Advise gentle cleansing of affected areas with soap and water, keeping lesions covered to reduce transmission. Educate parents on contagiousness and importance of hand hygiene and avoiding sharing towels or utensils. Exclude from daycare until 24 hours after starting treatment or until lesions are crusted and drying. Follow up in 7–10 days to ensure resolution.  
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 47-yr-old woman comes to the office because of an 8-wk history of a cough. She says the
cough is never productive, occurs at all times of the day (including at night), and is independent
of activity. She is not sure whether she had an upper respiratory tract infection preceding the
cough. She does recall that a new neighbor, who is a smoker, moved into a downstairs
apartment at the time the cough began. The neighbor frequently smokes outside the patient's
apartment window, triggering the cough.
She has not noticed any heartburn or runny nose. One month after the cough started, she
noticed pain at the right side of her breastbone occurring with stretching and deep breathing. At
that same time, she also noted that she has been wheezing during exertion. She has never had
wheezing before. She has had no shortness of breath.

Review of Systems:
General: Positive for 5- to 7-lb intentional weight loss via use of a FitBit¬Æ activity tracker. No
fever, chills, or malaise. Appetite normal.

Skin: No rashes

HEENT: Feels congested at night. No vision or hearing changes.

Pulmonary: Cough and wheezing as per history of present illness.

Cardiovascular: Sharp, right-sided chest pain occurring with stretching, coughing, and deep
breathing and lasting a second or two. No chest pain during exertion.

Gastrointestinal: Intermittent heartburn in the past but no recent episodes.

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Musculoskeletal: Sternal pain as per history of present illness. No edema or pain in extremities.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Hypertension, hypothyroidism due to thyroidectomy 12 yr ago for a benign
nodule, uterine cancer with hysterectomy 4 yr ago, and bipolar disorder. No known pulmonary
or cardiac disease.

Surgical history: Thyroidectomy (12 yr ago), hysterectomy (4 yr ago).

Medications: Losartan, verapamil, levothyroxine, aripiprazole, bupropion, escitalopram, and
topiramate.

Allergies: Intolerance to lurasidone (hand tremors) and oxycodone (nausea and vomiting).

Family history: No family history of lung cancer.

Social history: Life-long nonsmoker. Uses alcohol socially. Has never used illicit drugs. Works in
a hospital business office. Divorced; no sexual contact for 8 yr. Lives in Maryland. Has not
traveled outside the East Coast for 20 yr; has never traveled outside the US. No sick close
contacts.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Well-appearing woman; not in respiratory distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 36.8° C
Pulse: 79 beats/min
BP: 133/88 mm Hg
Respirations: 15/min
Pulse oximetry: 95% on room air

Skin: No cyanosis, rashes, or other lesions.

HEENT: Anicteric sclerae, pupils equally round and reactive to light. No nasal polyps.
Oropharynx clear, no postnasal drip. No lymphadenopathy.

Pulmonary: Normal respiratory effort. Good air entry and exit but bilateral wheezing noted
during forced expiration. No crackles or rhonchi.

Cardiovascular: Normal rate, regular rhythm. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Jugular venous
pressure not elevated.

Gastrointestinal: Soft, nontender, nondistended abdomen with normal bowel sounds.

Genitourinary: Not assessed

Musculoskeletal: Tender to palpation at the junction of the sternum and right 3rd and 4th ribs.
No swelling, redness, or tenderness in the legs.

Neurologic: Normal gait with no focal deficits in strength or sensation.

Mental status: Appropriate. Alert and oriented.

Test Results:
Results of pulmonary function testing return and show the following:
On room air:
● Normal forced vital capacity (FVC)
● Forced expiratory volume in 1 sec (FEV1): 60% of predicted

● Peak expiratory flow (PEF): 65% of predicted
After administration of inhaled albuterol:
● FEV1: 80%
● PEF: 75%
Findings are consistent with reactive airway disease, possibly cough-variant asthma.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 47  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Non-productive cough for 8 weeks, worse with environmental smoke exposure, associated with exertional wheezing and recent onset of right-sided sternal pain.  
Analysis: The patient presents with a chronic non-productive cough, bilateral wheezing on exam, and objective evidence of airflow obstruction on pulmonary function tests (FEV1 60% predicted) with partial reversibility after bronchodilator (FEV1 improved to 80% predicted). These findings strongly support a diagnosis of reactive airway disease, most consistent with cough-variant asthma. The temporal association with exposure to secondhand smoke from a neighbor suggests an environmental trigger. The absence of fever, sputum production, or systemic symptoms makes infectious etiologies unlikely. The sternal pain at the right 3rd and 4th costosternal junctions is likely musculoskeletal, given its reproducibility on palpation and lack of systemic signs. The wheezing, which is new and exertional, along with partial reversibility on spirometry, points to underlying airway hyperresponsiveness rather than cardiac or structural pulmonary disease. Differential considerations include gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), upper airway cough syndrome (UACS), and non-asthmatic eosinophilic bronchitis, but the patient lacks heartburn, postnasal drip, or sputum, and has objective evidence of obstructive pattern with reversibility, which favors asthma.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Chronic cough and wheezing with partial reversibility on spirometry are consistent with cough-variant asthma, likely triggered by environmental tobacco smoke. The sternal pain is musculoskeletal in origin.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  
Recommendations: Initiate a trial of inhaled corticosteroids (e.g., fluticasone propionate 220 mcg one puff twice daily) with as-needed albuterol for symptom relief. Counsel on avoidance of secondhand smoke exposure, including sealing windows or using air purifiers. Reassess symptom control in 4–6 weeks. Consider eucapnic voluntary hyperventilation or methacholine challenge testing if diagnosis remains uncertain. Address musculoskeletal pain with acetaminophen or NSAIDs as needed and reassurance. Continue monitoring for any signs of progression to more typical asthma (e.g., dyspnea, nocturnal symptoms).  
Notes: None

Vignette:
An 8-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician by her mother for intense itching that has been worsening over the past 2 weeks. The itching is particularly severe at night and disrupts her sleep. Her mother reports that her younger brother and father have recently developed similar itching. On examination, there are numerous small erythematous papules and excoriations in the interdigital web spaces of both hands, the flexor surfaces of the wrists, the axillary folds, and the periumbilical area. Several short, linear burrows approximately 5 to 10 mm in length are visible in the web spaces between the fingers. The face and scalp are spared. There are no vesicles or bullae. A mineral oil preparation from a burrow scraping examined under microscopy reveals mites, eggs, and fecal pellets.

Sex: Female

Analysis: The clinical presentation is highly consistent with scabies, characterized by intense pruritus, especially at night, and involvement of typical sites such as interdigital web spaces, flexor surfaces of wrists, axillae, and periumbilical area. The presence of linear burrows and family members with similar symptoms strongly supports person-to-person transmission. Microscopic identification of mites, eggs, and fecal pellets from a burrow scraping confirms the diagnosis. Differential diagnoses such as allergic contact dermatitis, eczema, or insect bites are less likely due to the distribution, burrows, and positive microscopy.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Confirmed case of scabies based on clinical features and microscopic evidence of Sarcoptes scabiei.

Sex: Not specified  
Complaint: Sudden onset of sharp, constant left-sided chest pain radiating to the center of the chest, associated with dyspnea and chills, unrelieved by naproxen.  
Analysis: The patient presents with acute-onset pleuritic-like chest pain, tachycardia, and dyspnea, without exertional exacerbation or typical cardiac risk factors. Key findings include a normal ECG (not shown but implied to be non-ischemic), normal troponin I (0.05 ng/mL, within normal limits), and a positive D-dimer (395 ng/mL). The most critical finding is the CT angiogram showing filling defects in bilateral segmental pulmonary arteries, confirming pulmonary embolism (PE). Her history of intermittent left leg swelling raises concern for undiagnosed deep vein thrombosis (DVT) as the source. Absence of trauma, immobilization, or known clotting disorder does not exclude venous thromboembolism (VTE), especially given her anemia (Hb 9.7 g/dL) possibly due to menorrhagia, which may contribute to hypercoagulability. Differential diagnoses such as acute coronary syndrome (ruled out by normal troponin and lack of ECG changes), pneumonia (no fever, cough, or lung findings), pericarditis (no positional pain, friction rub, or ECG changes), and musculoskeletal pain (no reproducible tenderness) are less likely.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Acute bilateral pulmonary embolism is confirmed by CT angiography, likely originating from a lower extremity deep vein thrombosis, given prior leg symptoms.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  
Recommendations: Initiate immediate anticoagulation with parenteral heparin (e.g., unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin) followed by transition to oral anticoagulant (e.g., direct oral anticoagulant or warfarin) for at least 3–6 months. Assess for need for ICU admission based on hemodynamic stability; although currently stable, tachycardia and bilateral PE warrant close monitoring. Evaluate for underlying hypercoagulable state and consider lower extremity Doppler ultrasound to confirm DVT. Address iron-deficiency anemia with iron supplementation and gynecologic follow-up for menorrhagia. Avoid NSAIDs due to GI and renal risks, especially with ongoing anticoagulation.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 72  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Acute confusion, fever, decreased oral intake, and urinary symptoms in a man with benign prostatic hyperplasia, now with signs of septic shock and urinary retention.  
Analysis: The patient presents with acute delirium, fever, hypotension (systolic BP 76 mmHg, MAP 55), tachycardia, tachypnea, and elevated lactate (5.8 mmol/L), meeting criteria for septic shock. Key findings include suprapubic tenderness, distended bladder, and 800 mL of cloudy, foul-smelling urine on catheterization, indicating urinary retention with pyuria and bacteriuria. Labs show leukocytosis with left shift (WBC 24,800/mcL, 22% bands), acute kidney injury (creatinine 3.2 mg/dL vs. baseline 1.2), thrombocytopenia (82,000/mcL), and markedly elevated procalcitonin (48 ng/mL), all consistent with severe systemic infection. Urinalysis confirms pyuria and bacteriuria. SOFA score of 11 indicates profound organ dysfunction. The clinical picture is most consistent with sepsis secondary to acute bacterial prostatitis or obstructive pyelonephritis in the context of urinary retention, likely exacerbated by recent UTI and BPH. Differential considerations include severe pneumonia or intra-abdominal infection, but urinary source is strongly supported by physical and laboratory findings.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: This is a case of septic shock secondary to a genitourinary infection, likely obstructive pyelonephritis or complicated prostatitis, in the setting of urinary retention and benign prostatic hyperplasia.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease  
Recommendations: Continue broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or carbapenem depending on local resistance patterns), ongoing IV fluid resuscitation, vasopressors if hypotension persists despite fluids, and close monitoring in ICU. Ensure adequate urinary drainage with indwelling catheter; consider nephrostomy or urology consultation if drainage is inadequate. Monitor lactate trend, renal function, and platelets. Adjust antibiotics based on culture results. Evaluate for source control and rule out abscess or obstructive uropathy with renal ultrasound if not already performed. Address delirium with non-pharmacologic measures and avoid sedatives.  
Notes: Despite initiation of antibiotics and catheterization, ongoing hemodynamic instability requires vasopressor support and ICU-level care. Prognosis is guarded given high SOFA score and multi-organ dysfunction.

- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,

Vignette:
A 38-year-old man is brought in by ambulance after sudden onset of severe vertigo, diplopia, and difficulty swallowing while at work 90 minutes ago. He has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. On examination, he is alert but dysarthric. Vital signs: T 37.0C, HR 78, RR 16, BP 168/94, SpO2 98%. Neurological exam reveals left-sided Horner syndrome, right-sided limb ataxia, decreased pain and temperature sensation on the left face and right body, and absent gag reflex on the left. CT head is negative for hemorrhage. CT angiography reveals left vertebral artery occlusion. NIHSS score is 12.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 38  
Sex: Not specified  
Complaint: Sudden onset of vertigo, diplopia, dysphagia, dysarthria, and neurological deficits including ataxia and sensory loss.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation is consistent with a dorsolateral medullary infarction (Wallenberg syndrome) due to left vertebral artery occlusion. Key findings include ipsilateral Horner syndrome, ataxia, and absent gag reflex, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation (left face, right body), indicating lateral medullary involvement. The presence of dysarthria, diplopia, and vertigo further supports brainstem ischemia. The NIHSS score of 12 confirms moderate to severe neurological deficit. CT head ruled out hemorrhage, and CTA confirmed left vertebral artery occlusion, establishing the ischemic etiology. Differential considerations include other posterior circulation strokes (e.g., basilar artery occlusion), demyelination, or brainstem tumor, but acute arterial occlusion on imaging and clinical course strongly favor ischemic stroke.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Acute ischemic stroke in the territory of the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) due to left vertebral artery occlusion, consistent with Wallenberg syndrome.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Neurology  
Recommendations: Immediate neurology consultation for acute stroke management. Initiate antithrombotic therapy (aspirin) unless contraindicated. Consider endovascular thrombectomy evaluation if within the extended time window and imaging supports salvageable tissue, though vertebral occlusion may limit accessibility. Start stroke protocol: monitor BP, avoid hypotension, manage dysphagia with NPO status and speech-language pathology evaluation, prevent aspiration, and admit to stroke unit. Initiate secondary stroke prevention after workup (lipid panel, echocardiogram, ECG, carotid imaging) to assess for underlying etiology (e.g., dissection, cardioembolic source).  
Notes: None

Age: 68  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: A 68-year-old man with known mild heart failure presents with worsening dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, lower extremity edema, weight gain, and fatigue over the past week despite medication adherence and prior diuretic escalation.  
Analysis: The patient has a history of coronary artery disease, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and mitral regurgitation, but his current presentation of progressive heart failure symptoms, biatrial enlargement, restrictive diastolic pattern on echocardiography (E/A >2, low e’ velocities), and normal LVEF (55%) suggests heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). However, the presence of severe concentric LV hypertrophy, unexplained by hypertension (BP is low), and systemic features such as mild macroglossia and fatigue raises suspicion for an infiltrative cardiomyopathy. The definitive finding of amorphous pink deposits with apple-green birefringence on Congo red staining of fat pad biopsy confirms systemic amyloidosis, most likely light-chain (AL) type given his history of monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS). The elevated BNP (1420 pg/mL) supports significant ventricular strain, while normal troponin argues against acute myocardial infarction. The absence of pericardial thickening rules out constrictive pericarditis. Pulmonary findings (crackles, pleural effusions) are consistent with congestive heart failure due to restrictive physiology from cardiac amyloidosis.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: This patient’s worsening heart failure symptoms are due to cardiac involvement in systemic AL amyloidosis, likely progressing from his underlying MGUS, manifesting as a restrictive cardiomyopathy with bilateral pleural effusions and systemic signs (macroglossia, edema).  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Cardiology  
Recommendations:  
- Immediate hematology consultation for confirmation of AL amyloidosis (serum free light chains, immunofixation electrophoresis, bone marrow biopsy) and initiation of chemotherapy if confirmed.  
- Avoid calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, and digoxin, which can worsen conduction abnormalities or heart failure in amyloidosis.  
- Optimize diuresis with furosemide under close monitoring of renal function and electrolytes; avoid over-diuresis due to risk of hypotension.  
- Monitor for arrhythmias; consider cardiology-directed evaluation for pacemaker if conduction disease progresses.  
- Evaluate for autonomic dysfunction given orthostatic dizziness and prior syncope.  
- Discontinue nitroglycerin if contributing to hypotension (BP 92/64 mm Hg).  
- Supportive care: low-sodium diet, fluid restriction if hyponatremic, daily weight monitoring.  
Notes: Cardiac amyloidosis carries a poor prognosis if untreated; early hematologic intervention is critical. Biopsy-proven amyloidosis with cardiac involvement requires urgent multidisciplinary management.

Complaint: Persistent heartburn and acid regurgitation for 6 months, worse after meals and at night, partially responsive to omeprazole 20 mg daily, with associated nocturnal cough and dental enamel erosion.

Differential considerations include non-erosive reflux disease, functional heartburn, and, less likely, peptic ulcer disease given mild epigastric tenderness. Obesity and alcohol use are contributing risk factors.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Upper endoscopy

Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology  
Recommendations: Refer to gastroenterology for upper endoscopy to evaluate for esophagitis, Barrett’s esophagus, or other complications. Consider increasing omeprazole to 20 mg twice daily or switching to another PPI for better symptom control. Continue lifestyle modifications (weight loss, avoid alcohol, no meals within 3 hours of bedtime, elevate head of bed). Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman presents with pain on the index finger of her left hand after accidentally touching a hot pan while cooking approximately 1 hour ago. She ran the finger under cool water immediately. She denies blistering, numbness, or limited range of motion. On examination, there is diffuse erythema of the palmar surface of the left index finger from the fingertip to the proximal interphalangeal joint. The skin is intact with no blistering or blanching. The area is tender to light touch and warm. Capillary refill is less than 2 seconds. Sensation and range of motion of the finger are intact.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 28  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Pain and erythema of the left index finger after thermal injury from a hot pan, with intact skin and no blistering.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation is consistent with a superficial partial-thickness burn (first-degree burn) involving the palmar surface of the left index finger. Key findings supporting this diagnosis include acute onset after thermal exposure, diffuse erythema, tenderness to light touch, warmth, intact skin without blistering or disruption, preserved capillary refill (<2 seconds), and normal sensation and range of motion. The absence of blanching, blistering, or deeper tissue involvement suggests the injury is limited to the epidermis. Differential considerations include early superficial partial-thickness burn (which may evolve), contact dermatitis, or localized infection (e.g., early cellulitis), but the clear temporal association with thermal exposure, lack of discharge or systemic signs, and intact skin make these less likely.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Acute, superficial (first-degree) thermal burn of the left index finger, limited to the palmar surface, without signs of deeper tissue injury or complications.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Emergency  
Recommendations: Continue cooling with cool (not cold) water if within first few hours; avoid ice. Recommend over-the-counter analgesics (e.g., acetaminophen or ibuprofen) for pain. Keep the area clean and dry; apply a topical antibiotic ointment (e.g., bacitracin) if desired, though not strictly necessary for first-degree burns. Cover with a non-adherent dressing only if exposed to contaminants. Advise monitoring for signs of infection (increasing redness, swelling, pus, fever) or progression to blistering (indicating possible second-degree burn). No restriction in activity is needed. Follow-up is not required unless symptoms worsen.  
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 20-year-old female college student presents with bilateral itchy, watery eyes for the past 3 days. She reports that the symptoms began shortly after spring pollen counts increased. She has a known history of seasonal allergies but has not yet started any medications this year. She denies eye pain, photophobia, purulent discharge, or changes in vision. Age: 10  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Recurrent nausea and dizziness during car rides, especially on winding roads, lasting 15–20 minutes after stopping, without vomiting or symptoms outside of travel.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation is consistent with motion sickness, a common vestibular disorder in children triggered by conflicting sensory inputs during motion. Key supporting features include age (peak incidence in childhood), symptom onset during car travel, absence of vomiting, resolution shortly after motion cessation, partial relief with visual stabilization (looking out window, sitting in front seat), and normal neurological and otoscopic exams. The absence of red flags—such as headaches, hearing loss, tinnitus, persistent vertigo, or neurological deficits—makes more serious central or inner ear pathology (e.g., vestibular neuritis, brain tumor, migraine variants) unlikely. Differential considerations include vestibular migraine and benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood, but these typically present with spontaneous episodes unrelated to motion and often include vertigo. This case lacks such features.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: The patient has motion sickness based on characteristic history and normal physical examination. No underlying neurological or otologic pathology is evident.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  
Recommendations: Reassure parents and patient that symptoms are consistent with benign motion sickness. Advise non-pharmacologic strategies: sitting in the front seat, focusing on the distant horizon, avoiding reading or screen use during travel, ensuring adequate ventilation, and minimizing travel on winding roads when possible. Consider over-the-counter options such as dimenhydrinate or meclizine 30–60 minutes before travel if symptoms significantly interfere with activities, following pediatric dosing guidelines. Encourage gradual exposure to motion to promote habituation.

A 50-year-old man presents with intermittent burning sensation in the substernal area that he has experienced occasionally over the past several weeks. The burning typically occurs 30 to 60 minutes after large meals, particularly those that are spicy or high in fat. The discomfort is relieved within minutes by over-the-counter antacids. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, hematemesis, or melena. He has no cardiac history. On examination, vital signs are normal. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended. There is no epigastric tenderness. Cardiac exam is unremarkable.

Sex: Not specified  
Complaint: Intermittent substernal burning after large, fatty, or spicy meals, relieved by antacids, without alarm symptoms.  
Analysis: The patient presents with classic symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), characterized by substernal burning that occurs postprandially—especially after large or fatty/spicy meals—and is relieved by antacids. The differential diagnosis includes GERD (most likely), non-cardiac chest pain, and less likely conditions such as peptic ulcer disease or esophagitis. Cardiac causes are less probable given the meal-related timing, lack of cardiac history, and absence of risk factors or concerning features on exam.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None

Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology

baseline_protocol:
Age: 12  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Intermittent mild upper back pain and stiffness for one year, not limiting activity and not associated with trauma, fever, or neurologic symptoms.  
Analysis: The patient presents with chronic, mild thoracic back discomfort and stiffness, with physical examination revealing asymmetric shoulder and scapular alignment and a mild right thoracic and left lumbar curvature. The spine x-ray confirms scoliosis with a Cobb angle of 11°, which is below the threshold for active intervention. The absence of neurologic deficits, systemic symptoms (e.g., fever, weight loss, night pain), joint swelling, or trauma makes infectious, inflammatory, or malignant causes unlikely. The lack of joint hypermobility, normal limb proportions, and absence of dysmorphic features argue against connective tissue or congenital disorders. The mild paraspinous tenderness and postural asymmetry are consistent with early adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, the most common form in this age group. Differential considerations include postural back pain, Scheuermann’s kyphosis, and musculoskeletal strain, but imaging does not support structural abnormalities beyond mild scoliosis.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Mild adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (Cobb angle 11°) is the most likely explanation for the patient’s intermittent upper back symptoms, with no evidence of neurologic, systemic, or structural pathology requiring immediate intervention.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics  
Recommendations: Reassure the patient and family that the scoliosis is mild and does not require treatment at this time. Recommend routine monitoring with annual clinical and spinal examinations to assess for curve progression, especially during growth spurts. Encourage normal physical activity and good posture. Consider repeat spine imaging if symptoms worsen, curve becomes more apparent on exam, or during periods of rapid growth. Educate the family about signs of progression (e.g., increasing asymmetry, shoulder imbalance, rib hump). No bracing or referral to orthopedics is indicated at this time given the Cobb angle <20°.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 19-year-old female college student is brought in by her roommate with a 24-hour history of high fever, diffuse rash, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, and progressive lightheadedness. She reports using a menstrual tampon that she forgot to change for approximately 3 days. On examination, she appears acutely ill with a diffuse, blanching, erythematous macular rash resembling a sunburn covering the trunk and extremities, including the palms and soles. Vital signs: T 40.2C, HR 136, RR 26, BP 72/40, SpO2 94%. Mucous membranes are hyperemic. Pelvic exam reveals a retained tampon, which is removed, and there is no evidence of abscess. Labs: WBC 15,400/mcL, platelets 88,000/mcL, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, AST 245 U/L, ALT 198 U/L, CK 1,240 U/L. Blood cultures are drawn and empiric clindamycin and vancomycin are initiated.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 19  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: 24-hour history of high fever, diffuse rash, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, lightheadedness, and recent prolonged tampon use.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation is highly consistent with toxic shock syndrome (TSS), a toxin-mediated illness most commonly associated with Staphylococcus aureus and prolonged tampon use. Key findings supporting this diagnosis include high fever (40.2°C), hypotension (72/40 mmHg), diffuse blanching macular rash involving palms and soles, mucous membrane hyperemia, and multiorgan involvement (elevated creatinine, transaminitis, rhabdomyolysis with elevated CK, thrombocytopenia). The history of a retained tampon for 3 days is a major risk factor. Differential diagnoses include streptococcal TSS, septic shock from another source, viral exanthems, or drug reactions; however, the temporal relationship with tampon use and the characteristic rash strongly favor staphylococcal TSS.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: This patient presents with classic signs and symptoms of toxic shock syndrome likely due to prolonged tampon retention, resulting in systemic toxin exposure, multiorgan dysfunction, and septic shock.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease  
Recommendations: Continue empiric clindamycin (to suppress toxin production) and vancomycin (for MRSA coverage) as initiated. Ensure prompt source control with retained tampon removal (already done). Begin aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation for hypotension and acute kidney injury. Monitor urine output, electrolytes, and organ function closely. Consider ICU admission for hemodynamic monitoring and possible vasopressor support. Do not delay treatment while awaiting blood culture results. Educate patient on proper tampon use and TSS prevention upon recovery.  
Notes: None

Complaint: Progressive wheezing and respiratory distress for 8 hours unresponsive to frequent albuterol use, with signs of severe respiratory compromise.

criterion:

Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.

Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 53-yr-old woman comes to the office because of palpitations. She is a current patient there
and has a history of well-controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and tension headaches. She
states that she has noticed intermittent palpitations over the past 2 mo. She describes the
episodes as a sensation of irregular and racing heartbeats that are accompanied by fatigue.
She denies any chest pain, shortness of breath, light-headedness, or syncope. The episodes
last from 10 min to several hours, occur once or twice/wk, and resolve on their own. The last
episode was 3 days ago. She cannot identify any particular triggers. She is generally active and
walks 3 miles several days/wk without any exertional symptoms including chest pain and
dyspnea. She has no family history of early cardiac disease or sudden death. She denies any
recent fever or infectious symptoms.

Review of Systems:
General: Patient has generally been feeling fine.

Skin: No new rashes or skin lesions.

HEENT: No vision changes, ear pain, nasal symptoms, or sore throat.

Pulmonary: Denies shortness of breath, dyspnea during exertion, and cough.

Cardiovascular: No orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or lower-extremity edema.

Gastrointestinal: Denies abdominal pain and poor appetite.

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Reproductive: Noncontributory

Musculoskeletal: No recent injury.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Has been generally in good spirits; no extremes of mood.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and tension headaches.

Surgical history: Appendectomy at age 20.

Medications: Lisinopril 10 mg daily and metformin 500 mg bid.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Mother is alive and has hypertension and diabetes mellitus. Father died of lung
cancer. No history of early coronary artery disease or sudden cardiac death.

Social history: Patient is married and works as a school teacher. Regularly exercises 3
times/wk. No history of smoking. Drinks a glass of wine with dinner most nights and one cup of
coffee each morning. Denies use of decongestants, cocaine, and other stimulants. No illicit drug
use.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Slender middle-aged woman in no apparent distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37.2° C
Pulse: 58 beats/min
BP: 125/74 mm Hg
Respirations: 14/min
Oxygen saturation: 96% on room air

Skin: No rashes noted.

HEENT: Oropharynx clear.

Pulmonary: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. No wheeze, rhonchi, or rales.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Brisk carotid upstrokes. No jugular venous distention.

Gastrointestinal: Soft, nontender, nondistended abdomen; positive bowel sounds.

Genitourinary: Unremarkable

Musculoskeletal: Unremarkable

Neurologic: Unremarkable

Mental status: Unremarkable
baseline_protocol:
Age: 53  
Sex: Woman  
Complaint: Intermittent palpitations described as irregular and racing heartbeats, lasting 10 minutes to several hours, occurring once or twice weekly over the past 2 months, associated with fatigue but no chest pain, dyspnea, lightheadedness, or syncope.  
Analysis: The patient presents with classic symptoms of paroxysmal arrhythmia, most concerning for atrial fibrillation or another supraventricular tachycardia, given the description of intermittent, self-terminating episodes of irregular and rapid heartbeat. Despite a normal resting pulse (58 bpm) and unremarkable cardiovascular exam with regular rhythm at the time of visit, the episodic nature of symptoms suggests intermittent arrhythmia not captured during examination. Key risk factors include age, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes, which increase the likelihood of atrial fibrillation. Differential diagnoses include sinus tachycardia, paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT), premature atrial or ventricular contractions, and non-cardiac causes such as anxiety or caffeine, though the latter are less likely given the specific description and absence of psychological symptoms or excessive stimulant use. The absence of red flag symptoms (e.g., syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, orthopnea) lowers immediate risk of hemodynamic instability or structural heart disease.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Ambulatory ECG monitoring (e.g., 24-48 hour Holter monitor or longer-term event recorder), TSH level to rule out hyperthyroidism, basic metabolic panel including electrolytes, and HbA1c to assess diabetes control.  
Conclusion: A 53-year-old woman with well-controlled hypertension and diabetes presents with recurrent, self-limited episodes of palpitations suggestive of paroxysmal arrhythmia, most likely atrial fibrillation or another supraventricular tachycardia, requiring ambulatory rhythm monitoring for definitive diagnosis.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Cardiology  
Recommendations: Initiate ambulatory ECG monitoring (e.g., 48-hour Holter or 2-week event monitor) to correlate symptoms with rhythm. Check TSH, electrolytes, renal function, and HbA1c. Counsel patient to avoid potential triggers such as alcohol and caffeine, though current intake is moderate. Continue current medications (lisinopril and metformin) as tolerated. If arrhythmia is confirmed, further evaluation for stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc score) and need for rate or rhythm control will be determined. No anticoagulation is indicated at this time without confirmed atrial fibrillation.  
Notes: The absence of symptoms at the time of examination underscores the need for prolonged rhythm monitoring. A single normal ECG or pulse does not exclude significant arrhythmia.

Diagnosis10: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with acute exacerbation, unspecified

He reports his sputum has changed from white to yellow-green. He denies fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, or significant increase in cough frequency. He is currently using tiotropium and an albuterol rescue inhaler as needed. Vital signs show temperature 98.6°F, heart rate 82, blood pressure 134/78, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 93% on room air (baseline 94-95%). On examination, there is mild bilateral expiratory wheezing without accessory muscle use. He is speaking in full sentences comfortably.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 20-year-old female college student who recently started a running program presents with bilateral dull, aching pain along the front of both shins. The pain began about 1 week ago and occurs primarily during and shortly after running, then resolves with rest. She runs on paved surfaces in her current athletic shoes that are over a year old. She denies pain at rest, nighttime pain, swelling, or history of stress fractures. On examination, there is mild tenderness on palpation along the medial border of the bilateral tibias spanning approximately 5 cm. There is no point tenderness, edema, or erythema. Ankle range of motion and strength are normal.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 20  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Bilateral dull, aching shin pain during and after running, resolving with rest, with tenderness along the medial tibial border.  
Analysis: The patient presents with activity-related bilateral shin pain, localized tenderness along the medial border of the tibia without point tenderness, swelling, or neurological deficits. The absence of rest pain, night pain, or signs of infection or fracture supports a diagnosis of medial tibial stress syndrome (MTSS), commonly known as "shin splints." Key risk factors include recent initiation of a running program, running on hard surfaces, and use of worn athletic footwear. Differential diagnoses include stress fracture (less likely due to lack of point tenderness and pain resolution at rest), chronic exertional compartment syndrome (unlikely without exertional tightness or persistent pain after exercise), and vascular claudication (not supported by young age, normal pulses, or typical presentation).  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Bilateral medial tibial stress syndrome likely secondary to recent running initiation, hard running surfaces, and inadequate footwear.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics  
Recommendations: Advise temporary reduction or modification of running activity to allow symptom resolution. Recommend low-impact cross-training (e.g., swimming, cycling). Emphasize proper footwear evaluation and replacement of old running shoes. Consider use of shock-absorbing insoles. Encourage gradual return to running with a structured progression plan, avoiding sudden increases in intensity or duration. Implement calf and lower leg stretching and strengthening exercises. Apply ice after activity if soreness occurs. Educate on warning signs of progression (e.g., persistent pain at rest, localized point tenderness) that would necessitate reevaluation for stress fracture.  
Notes: None

baseline_protocol:
Age: 70  
Sex: Not specified  
Complaint: 18 hours of worsening right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and jaundice in a patient with prior choledocholithiasis.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation is consistent with acute cholangitis, characterized by Charcot’s triad (right upper quadrant pain, fever, jaundice) and progressing to Reynolds’ pentad with hypotension and altered mental status (implied by acutely ill appearance and rigors). Key findings include high fever (39.6°C), tachycardia (HR 118), hypotension (BP 88/52), leukocytosis with bandemia (WBC 22,600/mcL, 15% bands), elevated bilirubin (direct > indirect), elevated ALP and transaminases, and lactic acidosis (lactate 4.1 mmol/L), indicating systemic inflammatory response and early septic shock. Imaging confirms common bile duct dilation (14 mm) with a distal CBD stone and mild intrahepatic ductal dilation, consistent with obstructive cholangiopathy. Differential considerations include acute hepatitis, choledocholithiasis without infection, and sepsis from other sources, but the combination of biliary obstruction on ultrasound, biochemical cholestasis, and systemic signs of infection strongly favors cholangitis.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: This patient presents with acute cholangitis due to choledocholithiasis, likely recurrent, with evidence of sepsis and lactic acidosis, requiring urgent biliary decompression.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology  
Recommendations: Immediate resuscitation with intravenous fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem) covering gram-negative and anaerobic organisms, and urgent consultation for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) within 24 hours—ideally within 12 hours given septic features. Hemodynamic support with vasopressors if needed, ICU admission, and close monitoring of lactate, renal function, and mental status. Blood cultures have been drawn; await results to guide antibiotic therapy. Avoid delaying ERCP for additional imaging.  
Notes: Prior sphincterotomy increases risk for recurrent stone formation or incomplete clearance, but does not preclude successful ERCP. Early biliary drainage is critical to reduce morbidity and mortality.

Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

[3]
tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
case_text:
Vignette:
A 3-year-old girl is brought in by her mother with a low-grade fever of 37.8°C and small blisters noticed on her hands and feet since this morning. The mother also notes a few small sores inside the child's mouth. The child is eating and drinking well, though slightly fussier than usual. Several children at her daycare have had similar symptoms. On examination, there are scattered small vesicles on the palms, soles, and a few on the dorsal hands. Two shallow ulcers are seen on the buccal mucosa. The child is alert, playful, and well-hydrated.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 3 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Low-grade fever, oral sores, and small blisters on hands and feet in a daycare-attending child.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation of low-grade fever, oral ulcers, and vesicles on the palms and soles in a preschool-aged child with known exposure at daycare is highly consistent with hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD), typically caused by coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71. Key findings supporting this diagnosis include the characteristic distribution of lesions (hands, feet, mouth), presence of shallow oral ulcers, and mild systemic symptoms with preserved hydration and activity level. The benign course and lack of neurological or systemic complications further support a typical presentation. Differential diagnoses include herpangina (which lacks hand/foot lesions), herpetic gingivostomatitis (usually more severe oral involvement, perioral lesions, no palmar/plantar vesicles), and other viral exanthems, but the combined mucocutaneous pattern makes HFMD most likely.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: This is a classic, mild case of hand, foot, and mouth disease, likely viral and self-limited, occurring in a community setting with known exposure.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  
Recommendations: Supportive care is sufficient. Encourage oral hydration with cool, non-acidic fluids. Offer soft, bland foods to minimize oral discomfort. Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever or pain as needed. Avoid aspirin. Counsel the mother that the child is contagious, especially via respiratory droplets and fecal-oral route; emphasize hand hygiene and avoid daycare until fever resolves and vesicles dry (typically 7–10 days). Monitor for warning signs: worsening fever, lethargy, vomiting, dehydration, or neurological symptoms (e.g., ataxia, seizures), which would require urgent evaluation.  
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 68-yr-old woman comes to the office with her daughter because of a 4-mo history of gradually
increasing lethargy and worsening memory. Her daughter is concerned because the mother has
stopped remembering whether she has taken her regular medications. The daughter is worried
that her mother might not be safe to live on her own. Prior to 4 mo ago, the woman had been
very busy with community activities, which she has since stopped, and her daughter had not
noticed any memory difficulties. The daughter is not aware of any recent illnesses or injuries.

Review of Systems:
General: The patient says she feels tired all the time and is usually cold even now during the
summer. She has a poor appetite but has gained 5 kg in weight in the preceding 4 mo despite
decreased appetite. No fever, chills, headache, or body aches.

Skin: Her skin has become dry, and her hair is now coarse and sparse. No rash or itching.

HEENT: She reports fullness in her throat, and her daughter has noticed that her mother's
voice has become hoarse and her face appears puffy, particularly around the eyes. No difficulty
swallowing.

Pulmonary: The patient reports new exertional shortness of breath and needing to pause after
climbing 1/2 flight of stairs. No cough or wheezing.

Cardiovascular: She used to have occasional palpitations before but has had none for the last 2
mo. She denies chest pain, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

Gastrointestinal: The patient's bowel movements have decreased from daily to once every 3
to 4 days when using laxatives. She does not have any abdominal pain or vomiting. Her
appetite is decreased.

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Musculoskeletal: Her ankles and lower legs are more swollen than they used to be. She reports
fatigue and leg weakness when climbing stairs or getting up from a chair.

Neurologic: She has become slower at performing daily activities, and extra effort is required.
Her daughter has noticed that her mother has trouble remembering recent events, such as
whether she has taken her medications. She denies having focal weakness or sensory
abnormalities, tremor, or visual symptoms.

Psychiatric: Her mood is depressed and she often stays in bed, not going out of the house for
many days.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Hypertension diagnosed 10 yr ago and controlled with three antihypertensives.
Atrial fibrillation (AF) rate-controlled with bisoprolol; previous admission to hospital with a fast
AF complicated with acute left ventricular failure; cardioversion failed to restore sinus rhythm.

Surgical history: Appendectomy at the age of 19 yr, left carpal tunnel syndrome surgery 2 yr
ago.

Medications: Bisoprolol 5 mg once/day, ramipril 10 mg once/day, furosemide 40 mg once/day,
warfarin 3 mg once/day.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Mother had hypothyroidism and a stroke in her 80s. Father died of metastatic
colon cancer.

Social history: She eats a healthy balanced diet, and her only exercise is walking to nearby
shops twice a week. She used to work as a receptionist but retired 3 yr ago. She is a
nonsmoker and drinks alcohol only occasionally. She has not travelled abroad in the last 3 yr.

General appearance: The patient is wearing several layers of clothing including a wool sweater
despite it being 89° F outside. She has a dull facial expression, and she looks pale and tired.

Vital signs:

Temperature: 35.8° C
Pulse: 56 beats/min, irregular
BP: 120/90 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min

Skin: Skin is cool and dry, no cyanosis or rash. Hair is coarse and dry with noticeable loss of

Head CT: Normal

Age: 68  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: A 68-year-old woman presents with 4 months of progressive lethargy, memory decline, cold intolerance, weight gain despite poor appetite, constipation, hoarseness, facial puffiness, and lower extremity edema.  
Analysis: The patient presents with a classic constellation of symptoms and signs consistent with severe primary hypothyroidism. Key findings include fatigue, cognitive slowing, cold intolerance, weight gain, dry skin, coarse hair, eyebrow loss, hoarse voice, periorbital and lower extremity edema, bradycardia, delayed deep tendon reflexes, and constipation. Laboratory results confirm primary hypothyroidism with markedly elevated TSH (88 µIU/mL) and low free T4 (0.4 ng/dL). Positive TPO antibodies indicate autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto’s thyroiditis) as the likely etiology. The anemia (Hb 9.8 g/dL) is likely multifactorial, possibly due to hypothyroidism or chronic disease. The chest X-ray findings of cardiomegaly and bibasilar atelectasis may reflect fluid retention and reduced respiratory drive in hypothyroidism. The patient’s atrial fibrillation, previously present but now controlled with bisoprolol, may have improved due to bradycardia from hypothyroidism. Differential diagnoses such as depression, dementia, heart failure, or malignancy are less likely given the global metabolic slowing and confirmatory thyroid labs.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: The patient has severe primary hypothyroidism due to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, manifesting with systemic symptoms including cognitive impairment, bradycardia, myxedema-related edema, and metabolic slowing.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  
Recommendations:  
- Initiate levothyroxine replacement therapy at an appropriate dose, considering cautious dosing due to age, bradycardia, and underlying cardiovascular disease (atrial fibrillation, prior heart failure). A starting dose of 25–50 mcg daily is recommended.  
- Monitor for signs of cardiac decompensation or arrhythmia after initiation.  
- Recheck TSH and free T4 in 6–8 weeks after starting therapy to guide dose titration.  
- Evaluate and manage contributing factors: consider reducing or adjusting furosemide given edema may be myxedematous rather than purely congestive; ensure INR is monitored closely as warfarin metabolism may change with thyroid replacement.  
- Assess cognitive and functional status over time; improvement in mental status is expected with treatment.  
- Address depression with supportive care; consider psychiatric evaluation if mood does not improve with thyroid treatment.  
- Educate patient and daughter about the condition, expected symptom improvement timeline, and medication adherence.  
- Consider home safety evaluation given concerns about living independently.  
Notes: This case may represent myxedema (severe hypothyroidism), particularly given bradycardia, hypothermia, and edema. While not yet in myxedema coma, the patient requires urgent treatment due to multisystem involvement and functional decline.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 9 months  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Episodic inconsolable crying with legs drawn to abdomen, vomiting, and currant jelly stool in a 9-month-old infant.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for intussusception, including paroxysmal abdominal pain, vomiting, lethargy, and passage of currant jelly stool. Physical exam findings—palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant, empty right lower quadrant (Dance sign), and currant jelly stool on rectal exam—are highly suggestive. Abdominal ultrasound confirming a target sign (doughnut sign) in the right upper quadrant provides definitive imaging evidence of ileocolic intussusception. The absence of peritonitis or perforation supports a non-operative management approach. Differential diagnoses include gastroenteritis, malrotation with volvulus, and Henoch-Schönlein purpura, but the combination of symptoms, exam findings, and imaging makes intussusception the definitive diagnosis.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: A 9-month-old male with confirmed ileocolic intussusception based on clinical presentation and ultrasound, without signs of perforation or peritonitis, requiring prompt reduction.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery  
Recommendations: Proceed immediately with air enema reduction under radiologic guidance, as it is both diagnostic and therapeutic in uncomplicated intussusception. Ensure intravenous access and fluid resuscitation due to signs of dehydration and tachycardia (HR 168). Monitor vital signs closely during the procedure. If reduction is unsuccessful or perforation occurs, prepare for emergent surgical intervention (e.g., manual reduction or resection). Admit the patient for observation post-procedure regardless of success, and monitor for recurrence, bleeding, or signs of peritonitis.  
Notes: Air enema should not be delayed; however, it is contraindicated if peritonitis or perforation is present. Post-reduction, recurrence occurs in up to 10% of cases, typically within 24–48 hours.

Vignette:
A 70-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia presents to his primary care physician with a 3-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency. He reports mild suprapubic discomfort and low-grade fever of 100.4°F. He denies flank pain, rigors, or hematuria. His past medical history is notable for BPH managed with tamsulosin. On examination, he appears mildly uncomfortable but is in no acute distress. Vital signs show temperature 100.4°F, blood pressure 138/82, heart rate 78. Abdominal examination reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Digital rectal exam shows an enlarged, nontender prostate. Urinalysis demonstrates pyuria and positive nitrites.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 70  
Sex: Not specified  
Complaint: A 70-year-old man presents with 3 days of dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, mild suprapubic discomfort, and low-grade fever.  
Analysis: The patient has symptoms and urinalysis findings consistent with acute bacterial cystitis. Key findings include dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic tenderness, low-grade fever, pyuria, and positive nitrites on urinalysis—indicative of gram-negative bacteriuria. His history of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) on tamsulosin increases his risk for lower urinary tract symptoms and urinary stasis, predisposing to infection. Absence of flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, rigors, or high fever makes pyelonephritis less likely. Hematuria is denied, and the prostate is enlarged but nontender, making acute bacterial prostatitis less probable. The clinical picture most strongly supports uncomplicated acute cystitis in a male with risk factors.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: This is a case of acute bacterial cystitis in a 70-year-old man with BPH, based on urinary symptoms, low-grade fever, suprapubic tenderness, and urinalysis showing pyuria and positive nitrites.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Urology  
Recommendations: Initiate empirical antibiotic therapy for uncomplicated urinary tract infection (e.g., nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, depending on local resistance patterns and renal function), unless contraindicated. Avoid fluoroquinolones unless absolutely necessary due to side effect profile and resistance concerns. Consider urine culture to guide therapy, especially given male gender and age, which increase risk for complicated UTI. Ensure adequate hydration. Reassess in 48–72 hours for symptom improvement. If symptoms worsen or fail to improve, consider further evaluation including renal function tests, serum inflammatory markers, and imaging (e.g., renal ultrasound) to rule out complications such as prostatitis, abscess, or obstruction. Optimize BPH management with current tamsulosin and consider urology follow-up for recurrent infections.  
Notes: Male UTIs are often considered complicated due to higher risk of underlying pathology; close follow-up is essential.

Age: 40  
Sex: male  
Complaint: Crush injury to both lower extremities with severe pain, swelling, numbness, and oliguria with dark urine following 4-hour entrapment; signs of acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation is consistent with crush syndrome, a life-threatening complication of prolonged muscle compression leading to rhabdomyolysis, electrolyte disturbances, and acute kidney injury. Key findings include markedly elevated CK (124,000 U/L), myoglobinuria (dark brown urine, myoglobin 48,000 ng/mL), acute kidney injury (creatinine 3.4 mg/dL, oliguria), hyperkalemia (K+ 6.8 mEq/L with ECG changes), hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L), and hemodynamic instability (tachycardia, hypotension). These findings confirm systemic complications of rhabdomyolysis. Differential considerations include hypovolemic shock, acute tubular necrosis from other causes, and other causes of hyperkalemia, but the context of prolonged crush injury makes crush syndrome the definitive diagnosis.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: The patient has crush syndrome with severe rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, life-threatening hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis requiring immediate multidisciplinary critical care.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Emergency  
Recommendations: Continue aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with normal saline at 1.5 L/hr to maintain urine output >200–300 mL/hr. Maintain alkalinization with IV sodium bicarbonate to target urine pH >6.5. Continue IV calcium gluconate for cardioprotection; monitor ECG continuously. Administer additional treatments for hyperkalemia as needed (e.g., insulin + glucose, albuterol, kayexalate). Prepare for emergent hemodialysis due to severe hyperkalemia, oliguria, volume overload risk, and uremic complications. Monitor for compartment syndrome; surgical fasciotomy may be required if clinical signs progress. Correct hypocalcemia only if symptomatic or severe; avoid routine correction due to risk of precipitation during recovery phase. Monitor electrolytes, CK, renal function, and urine output hourly. Involve nephrology and trauma surgery early.  
Notes: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes is immediately life-threatening. Hemodialysis is likely required. Compartment syndrome must be assessed serially despite initial management.

Diagnosis10: Subarachnoid haemorrhage from anterior communicating artery
Vignette: A 47-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of the worst headache of her life that began 1 hour ago while straining during a bowel movement. She describes it as a thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds. She experienced one episode of vomiting and brief loss of consciousness. Non-contrast CT head reveals diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage in the basal cisterns. CT angiography identifies a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm.

Vignette:
A 47-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of the worst headache of her life that began 1 hour ago while straining during a bowel movement. She describes it as a thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds. She experienced one episode of vomiting and brief loss of consciousness. Her past medical history includes migraines and she is a current smoker. On examination, she is photophobic, irritable, and has a stiff neck. Vital signs: T 37.4C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 178/96, SpO2 98%. Neurological exam reveals intact cranial nerves, mild bilateral lower extremity weakness, and pronounced nuchal rigidity. Hunt and Hess grade III. Non-contrast CT head reveals diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage in the basal cisterns. CT angiography identifies a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm.
baseline_protocol:
